title: Cornell Just Wrote the Case for My Course. Then It Stopped.
author: Doan Winkel
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), September 25, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel responds to Cornell's 230-page Committee on the Future of the American University report, praising its diagnosis of college as a transaction but arguing it stops short of the mechanisms that sustain it. He agrees with the push for transformative education built on judgment, hands-on projects, and assessment that survives AI, and he sees his own mastery-based course as a working version of it. His central critique is the gradebook: points, weighted averages, rubrics, and late penalties keep the course a ledger, so students keep behaving like customers. He proposes removing points from artifacts, using complete or try again verdicts, treating time as the variable, and letting outside practitioners hold the verdict while the instructor coaches. On AI he argues for redesigning assignments so AI raises cognitive demand with a human check at the end, rather than restricting the tool. He closes that small mission-driven schools can act faster than Cornell and should prototype now instead of convening another forum.
points: The report correctly names the transactional nature of college, but it never identifies grading mechanics as the machinery that sustains that transaction.
Replacing points with complete-or-try-again verdicts and treating time as the variable pushes students to revise until the work is real.
Giving a practitioner the verdict while the instructor coaches makes student work hard to game and puts capacity on display for future employers.
Restricting AI protects old assignments, whereas redesigning assignments with process logs and live defence makes restriction unnecessary.
Diagnosis without a prototype is only a white paper, so small schools should pilot one course section for a semester rather than wait for committees.
quotes: College has become a transaction. Tuition in, credential out, credential to employer, job.
You can’t ask students to stop behaving like customers while the course keeps a cash register at the front of the room.
You can take the points off the artifact, the verdict becomes complete or try again, time becomes the variable, students revise until the work is real.
In my courses a founder, a designer, or a buyer (a subject-matter expert for the particular skill) looks at the artifact and says complete or try again. I coach, they judge.
Restricting the tool protects the old assignment. Redesigning the assignment makes the restriction unnecessary.
Diagnosis without a prototype is a white paper. The prototype is where you learn whether the diagnosis was right.
Then look at your own syllabus and find the transaction. It’s in the points, it’s in the participation grade and the late penalty and the extra credit.
